title: the sandals on the throne
hook: Bharata rules fourteen years with Rama's sandals on the throne
carry: touching feet is humility that asks a blessing

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama spent his one wish on forgiveness, and the Pushpaka rose. Your line was forgiveness is part of dharma. Today, the long road home, in reverse.

Over Kishkindha, Sita asks Rama for something. She wants the wives of the monkey leaders, Tara and the others, to come with them to Ayodhya and share the homecoming. So the Pushpaka comes down, and the women climb aboard in their best clothes. Rama agrees at once. The woman who spent months among strangers wants to arrive home surrounded by friends.

Then the flight north becomes the whole story, told backward. Rama points out the places: Rishyamuka, where he met Sugriva; Panchavati, where Ravana took Sita; Chitrakuta, where Bharata came to find him. They land at the sage Bharadvaja's hermitage on the day the fourteen years are complete, and Rama sends Hanuman ahead with a strange instruction: tell Bharata I'm coming, and watch his face. If, after fourteen years, he wants to keep the kingdom, let him have it. Some readers hear a test; others hear respect. Hanuman finds Bharata at Nandigram, outside the capital, living like a hermit in bark clothes. On the throne sit Rama's sandals. Years before, in the forest, Bharata begged Rama to come home, and when Rama wouldn't break his word to their father, Bharata asked for his sandals instead. He set them on the throne and ruled as their servant. Rama is coming, Hanuman tells him, and Bharata falls to the ground with joy. Why sandals? In Hindu tradition, the feet of the one you honor are holy. They're the lowest part of a person, so bowing to them says: I make myself small before you. That's why Hindus bow at the feet of God in the temple, why the padukas of gurus are kept and worshiped in shrines, and why children touch their elders' feet, especially on festival days, and get a blessing back. Bharata held a kingdom for fourteen years and called himself the servant of a pair of sandals.
screen: `THE EXILE UNROLLS BACKWARD.` · `WATCH BHARATA'S FACE.` · `RAMA'S SANDALS ON THE THRONE.` · `THE FEET OF THE ONE YOU HONOR.` · then, large: `THE SERVANT OF A PAIR OF SANDALS.`

segments.voice: Picture an elder in your life, or a teacher who shaped you. On festival days, many Hindu children bow and touch an elder's feet, and the elder blesses them. Bow your head a little where you sit, as if you were at their feet, and silently ask for their blessing. If you don't pray, simply let one long breath carry your thanks to them.
Paduka. Sandals: Rama's, set on the throne for fourteen years while Bharata ruled as their servant.
Your line: touching feet is humility that asks a blessing. Bharata lived it for fourteen years, bowing to a pair of sandals. That's day six hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: On Diwali and other festival days, many Hindu children touch the feet of their parents and elders and receive a blessing; in many lineages a guru's padukas, sandals, are kept in the shrine and worshiped.
